meta.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
meta.author: bank-team-english-literature
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify the function an epigraph performs in a translated edition.
questions.stem: Translator's note 3 explains that the epigraph above the first chapter of the river novel was chosen by the original author.

options.text: The epigraph introduces the theme by stating a thought the chapter will develop and complicate.
The epigraph frames the chapter by previewing the questions the narrative will take up and settling them.
options.misconception: assumes an epigraph settles the meaning of what follows

options.text: The epigraph identifies the source text so readers can check the translation against the original wording.
options.misconception: treats an epigraph as a bibliographic citation

options.text: The epigraph announces the dates of the story so readers can place the events on a calendar.
options.misconception: reads an epigraph as a factual dating device

questions.explanation: An epigraph opens a work by stating a position the text then tests, and the author's own choice signals deliberate framing. Preview and verdict, source citation
questions.hint: Ask what the chapter does with the epigraph's thought.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a translated title is reconciled with the novel's final page.
questions.stem: Note 7 on the street novel explains why the published English title differs from the original phrase translated word for word.

answer.exemplar: The literal rendering pointed towards a market day, but the novel's closing pages take place in a street emptied of market stalls, so the title in translation was changed to keep the sense of the ending intact. A translator must weigh a title's literal accuracy against the meaning the whole work eventually discloses, and here the ending won that weighing.

questions.explanation: A title must reach the meaning the ending finally discloses, so a translator may adjust a literal phrase to preserve that agreement. The choice here follows the final pages rather than the dictionary.
questions.hint: Ask what the last pages make the title mean.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse the payoff of a recurring image in the closing chapter.
questions.stem: In translator's note 11 on the harbour novel, the translator asks what the returning image of the swallowed coin achieves.

options.text: It pays off the motif by repeating the earlier image unchanged, so readers recognise the pattern and settle.
options.misconception: mistakes simple repetition for a payoff

options.text: It pays off the motif by closing the account the earlier chapters opened, so the coin holds the meaning.
It pays off the motif by shifting the image into a new context, so readers must revise its earlier meaning.
options.misconception: misses the completion the returning image delivers

options.text: It pays off the motif by naming the coin explicitly for the first time, so the payoff depends on identifying.
options.misconception: reduces the payoff to naming an object

questions.explanation: A motif pays off when its final appearance completes what earlier appearances set up, and the swallowed coin gathering the meaning of loss does that. Unchanged repetition, shifted context
questions.hint: Ask what the coin has been holding since the first chapter.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a described setting shapes the reader's emotional response.

stimulus.body: The harbour novel opens on the quay at first light with the tide out and the boats still moored, and the translator's draft described the light as thin. The publisher queried the word, and the translator defended it in the marginal note that follows.

questions.stem: Translator's note 14 explains why the word thin was kept in the rendering of the quay's early light.

options.text: It was kept since thin is a standard translator's choice for any weak light at dawn in a novel.
options.misconception: treats a rendering choice as house convention

options.text: It was kept since the original word meant narrow, and narrow was the only accurate rendering available.
options.misconception: reduces the choice to the closest dictionary equivalent

options.text: It was kept since thin describes the light's quality and also prepares a shortage running through the book.
It was kept since the publisher had approved the word and the translator did not want to reopen the query.
options.misconception: explains a literary choice by commercial convenience

questions.explanation: A word in a setting description carries literal and emotional work at once, and thin light signals both quality and the deprivation the novel develops. House convention, dictionary closeness
questions.hint: Ask what else the word predicts about the novel.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how two devices in a translation work together on one claim.
questions.stem: Translator's note 18 on the mill novel asks why the epigraph and the final chapter were arranged to echo each other.

options.text: Because the epigraph states the mill's motto and the last chapter repeats it, so the two devices confirm each.
options.misconception: reduces an echo to simple reinforcement

options.text: Because the epigraph names the narrator and the last chapter replaces him, so the devices track a change.
options.misconception: reads the pairing as a change of narrator only

options.text: Because the epigraph is short and the last chapter long
options.misconception: explains a pairing by comparing lengths of text

options.text: Because the epigraph states the mill's motto and the last chapter shows the motto abandoned, so the two argue.

questions.explanation: Two devices work together when the second turns the first into an argument, and a final chapter abandoning the opening motto makes the epigraph a position under challenge. Repetition, voice change
questions.hint: Ask what the ending does to the opening statement.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise understatement in a translation of a heightened claim.
questions.stem: Marginal note 21 records the translator's defence of the flat phrase hardly worth mentioning in the famine chapter.

options.text: The phrase understates since a huge event is said in tiny words, so readers feel the gap between them.
The phrase overstates since the translation renders a tiny event in enormous words, so readers feel the gap.
options.misconception: reverses understatement into overstatement

options.text: The phrase is simply unclear, since the translator has failed to find the right English word for the original.
options.misconception: explains the flatness as a translation problem

options.text: The phrase is ironic, since the event described is the most important in the novel.
options.misconception: collapses understatement into irony of priority

questions.explanation: Understatement means a large thing is said in small words, and hardly worth mentioning applied to a famine creates the gap readers register. Reversal, translation failure
questions.hint: Ask how small the words are against the size of the event.

questions.learningObjective: Identify who a text addresses and how the address shapes its reading.
questions.stem: Note 25 on the village novel records why the translator kept the second-person address in the letters chapter.

answer.exemplar: The letters chapter keeps its second-person address because the translator wanted the reader placed in the position of the person receiving them, which is the whole effect of the chapter. Once the address becomes a third-person report of letters, the reader stops being the recipient and the intimacy the original sustains is lost along with the address.

questions.explanation: Address determines readers' position inside the text, and second person makes the reader the recipient of the letters. Rendering the address in the third person turns the chapter into a report.
questions.hint: Ask who readers become when the address is kept.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether an epigraph is best understood as a key or a promise.
questions.stem: Translator's note 29 argues with a reviewer who wanted the epigraph of the orchard novel treated as a key to the ending.

options.text: The reviewer is right, since an epigraph by definition tells the reader the conclusion.
options.misconception: treats the epigraph as a statement of the ending

options.text: The reviewer is wrong, since an epigraph promises a direction and sets readers' expectations.
The reviewer is right, since the author said the epigraph referred to the final scene.
options.misconception: grounds the reading in unverifiable author testimony

options.text: The reviewer is wrong, since epigraphs in translated editions are inserted to advertise the book.
options.misconception: attributes epigraphs to marketing rather than to authors

questions.explanation: An epigraph frames a direction of inquiry and leaves the outcome open, which is why it sets expectations rather than announcing results. Definition, author testimony
questions.hint: Ask whether an epigraph settles what happens next.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse a title that is confirmed rather than contradicted by the ending.

stimulus.body: The title of the translated novel refers to a river that no longer reaches the sea. The last chapter describes a new channel cut through the fields, and the water that once vanished now arrives at the estuary. The translator was asked whether this confirms the title or undoes it.

questions.stem: Translator's note 33 explains how the ending should be read against the novel's title.

options.text: It confirms the title, since the title names the old arrangement while the ending records its replacement.
options.misconception: mistakes a change of circumstance for a matching title

options.text: It undoes the title, since the title promises a river that never arrives and the ending delivers one.
options.misconception: confirms the opposite of the intended reading

options.text: It confirms the title, since the ending restores the river the title describes, so the work ends as promised.
It leaves the title undecided, since a title naming a geographical feature cannot be confirmed by an ending.
options.misconception: treats titles as immune to narrative confirmation

questions.explanation: A title naming a dry river is confirmed when the ending restores the flow it described, and the new channel does that. Matching circumstance, undoing
questions.hint: Ask what the new channel does to the river in the title.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a motif's payoff from a coincidence introduced late.
questions.stem: Translator's note 37 asks whether the ladder found in the loft in the final chapter pays off the earlier mentions.

options.text: It pays off, since the ladder is an old and much used object, so it must have carried meaning throughout.
options.misconception: assumes age of an object implies accumulated significance

options.text: It does not pay off, since the earlier mentions were about a different ladder
options.misconception: invents an unrelated earlier object to break the pattern

options.text: It does not pay off, since payoffs must be stated openly in the text, and this one is left for the reader.
options.misconception: requires a payoff to be declared explicitly

options.text: It pays off, since the earlier mentions established the roof access and the last chapter turns

questions.explanation: A payoff gathers earlier mentions into a decisive use, and the loft ladder turning established roof access into the rescue route does that. Age of object, invented antecedent
questions.hint: Ask what the earlier mentions made possible.

questions.learningObjective: Identify how a change of setting registers a change of feeling.
questions.stem: Translator's note 41 on the asylum novel compares the bright ward of the opening with the winter yard of the last chapter.

options.text: The shift of setting carries the change in feeling, since the cold yard makes readers register the narrator's.
The shift of setting carries the change in feeling, since the bright ward makes the later yard seem worse.
options.misconception: attributes the effect to contrast rather than the new place

options.text: The shift of setting is decorative only, and the change in feeling comes entirely from the narrator's stated.
options.misconception: cuts the setting out of the emotional effect

options.text: The shift of setting signals a change of narrator, since a different place usually means a different speaker.
options.misconception: assumes a change of place implies a change of voice

questions.explanation: A setting carries emotional weight of its own, and the winter yard transmits the narrator's despair to the reader without narration of it. Contrast, decoration
questions.hint: Ask what the new place does to readers' feeling.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a title and an epigraph work together at the opening of a work.
questions.stem: Note 45 on the seed catalogue novel records how the title and the epigraph were chosen to point the same way.

answer.exemplar: The title names a ledger of debts owed to the land, and the epigraph quotes a line about counting what cannot be repaid. Together they tell the reader to approach the catalogue as an accounting of obligations rather than a record of stock, and the translator kept both unchanged because the alignment between them is what makes the family history in the middle chapters legible as a series of unpaid claims.

questions.explanation: When a title and an epigraph point the same way, the reader receives one instruction that the middle chapters test. The translator kept both since their alignment makes the history legible.
questions.hint: Ask what reading method the pairing tells the reader to use.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of an ironic understatement in a translated line.
questions.stem: Translator's note 49 defends the rendering of the phrase the damage was not serious in the flood chapter.

options.text: The phrase works as simple understatement since the damage really was minor compared with the losses.
options.misconception: treats ironic understatement as plain understatement

options.text: The phrase works ironically since the narrator says the damage was minor
The phrase works as a literal claim, since the translator found no word meaning anything but trivial damage.
options.misconception: reduces the phrase to a dictionary reading

options.text: The phrase works as praise, since a narrator who minimises a disaster is usually protecting the reader.
options.misconception: reads restraint as protective kindness

questions.explanation: A claim of minor damage contradicted by what the book has established is ironic understatement, since the gap carries a judgement the narrator refuses to state. Plain understatement, literal reading
questions.hint: Ask what the book has told the reader about the damage.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a change of address within a text alters the reader's role.

stimulus.body: In the courtroom novel the narrator speaks in the first person for two hundred pages, then switches to the third person for the final eleven and addresses the reader directly in a single closing paragraph. The translator preserved both shifts and marked them in the margin of the working copy.

questions.stem: Translator's note 52 explains what the final direct address does to the reader's position.

options.text: It confirms the shift the third person signalled, so the address simply names a change made.
options.misconception: treats the address as a label for the grammatical change

options.text: It withdraws the reader, since a text that turns to the third person has stopped assuming anyone is present.
options.misconception: confuses third person with absence of one

options.text: It moves the reader from listening to being addressed, so the closing claim lands as a personal summons.
It weakens the closing claim, since a direct address sounds personal and personal statements are less binding.
options.misconception: assumes personal phrasing reduces commitment

questions.explanation: Direct address repositions the reader from a listener into a recipient, so the closing claim arrives as a personal summons rather than a report. Naming a grammatical change, withdrawing the reader
questions.hint: Ask what readers are now being treated as.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how an epigraph establishes a problem for the text.
questions.stem: Translator's note 56 asks what problem the epigraph of the customs house novel sets for the reader.

options.text: It poses a problem of style, since the epigraph is written in a manner the novel never uses elsewhere.
options.misconception: reduces the epigraph to a question of register

options.text: It poses no problem, since an epigraph that raises a question without answering it is simply a device.
options.misconception: treats unanswered questions as decoration

options.text: It poses a problem of authorship, since the epigraph is signed by a name the novel later reveals to be false.
options.misconception: turns the epigraph's problem into a question of attribution

options.text: It poses a problem of measurement, since the epigraph questions who may count a journey

questions.explanation: An epigraph can pose the central question of a work and leave it open, and a challenge about counting journeys organises the novel. Register, atmosphere
questions.hint: Ask what question the epigraph refuses to answer.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the reading of a title that best fits the closing scene.
questions.stem: Translator's note 60 asks which title best suits the village novel that ends with two brothers walking away from each other.

options.text: The Salt Road suits it, since the two brothers leave by separate roads and never once cross again.
The Salt Road suits it, since the road through the village was salted in winter and appears in the final.
options.misconception: grounds the title in a literal detail of the ending

options.text: The Salt Road suits it, since salt was the family's trade and the title records their shared livelihood.
options.misconception: reads the title as a trade description rather than a fate

options.text: The Salt Road does not suit it, since a title
options.misconception: insists titles must describe people directly

questions.explanation: A title earns its place by carrying the work's final meaning, and two brothers parting along separate roads makes a road the image of a shared life now split. Literal detail, family trade
questions.hint: Ask what the title can name about the ending.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a motif's payoff reframes the reader's earlier reading.
questions.stem: Note 63 on the orchard novel asks how the final chapter's return of the pruning knife changes how the earlier chapters read.

answer.exemplar: The pruning knife appears in the earlier chapters as a working tool, and each use seems a small detail of country labour with no symbolic weight. In the last chapter the brother who left the orchard is holding the knife again, and it is the instrument by which the trees were cut down, so the motif's payoff recasts every earlier mention as the slow preparation of a destruction the reader had taken for routine.

questions.explanation: A payoff can retroactively change how earlier appearances are read, and a knife revealed as a destructive instrument makes prior details sinister. Only their significance is reorganised.
questions.hint: Ask what the knife was doing in the earlier chapters.

questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a change of setting is an emotional device or a structural one.
questions.stem: Translator's note 67 considers whether the move from the boarding house to the ship in the migration novel is emotional or structural.

options.text: It is only structural, since the emotional charge of a scene comes from the dialogue and never from the place.
options.misconception: excludes setting from emotional effect entirely

options.text: It is both, since the sea setting carries the migrants' fear
It is only emotional, since moving house mid novel happens for the sake of a mood and not to organise.
options.misconception: separates the two functions as exclusive

options.text: It is neither, since translators should preserve the original sequence of places without comment.
options.misconception: treats a question of effect as outside the translator's.

questions.explanation: A setting change can carry feeling and mark the work's structure at once, and the ship's deck does both here. Exclusive functions, dialogue-only emotion
questions.hint: Ask what the new place does beyond what the new chapter.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how an epigraph and a setting work together in an opening.

stimulus.body: The quarry novel opens with an epigraph about stones being patient, and then opens the first chapter in a quarry where the narrator describes the extraction of one particular block for eleven paragraphs. The translator kept the epigraph in place because the two devices seemed to be talking to each other.

questions.stem: Translator's note 71 explains how the epigraph and the opening setting work together.

options.text: They work together, since both devices describe quarry work and therefore repeat each other's content.
options.misconception: reduces a pairing to shared subject matter

options.text: They work separately, since an epigraph states a theme and a setting supplies place
options.misconception: assumes devices occupy sealed categories

options.text: They work together, since the epigraph's patience is given a counter-image in the block the quarry has chosen
They work separately, since the translator was asked
options.misconception: grounds the separation in an editorial instruction

questions.explanation: An epigraph and a setting can set up a tension, and patience answered by a block chosen for breaking makes the opening pair work as argument. Shared subject, sealed categories
questions.hint: Ask what the block does to the epigraph's claim.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how understatement shapes the reader's judgement of a narrator.
questions.stem: Translator's note 75 asks what the narrator's habit of minimising reveals about her.

options.text: It reveals a character who minimises to protect herself
options.misconception: redirects readers' judgement to the wrong target

options.text: It reveals nothing, since a habit of minimising is a normal way of speaking and carries no judgement.
options.misconception: treats a verbal habit as free of character meaning

options.text: It reveals that the translator has weakened the original, since the original narrator magnified every event.
options.misconception: invents an opposing original rather than reading the effect

options.text: It reveals a character who minimises to protect others

questions.explanation: A habitual minimiser is making a choice about who bears the weight of what is said, and reading the habit as protective yields a judgement about her character. Self-protection, no judgement
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from the things she refuses to name.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the audience a text's address presumes.
questions.stem: Translator's note 79 observes that the manual of the inland navigation is written to a reader who already knows the river.

options.text: It presumes one who shares the author's local knowledge, so the unexplained names and shortcuts are welcome.
It presumes one with no local knowledge, so the unexplained names invite the reader to learn the valley.
options.misconception: presumes an ignorant audience the text never addresses

options.text: It presumes one who shares the author's knowledge, so the omissions must be errors in the transmitted text.
options.misconception: treats an informed address as evidence of copying error

options.text: It presumes one who shares the author's knowledge, so the guide is worthless to anyone outside the region.
options.misconception: turns a local address into a judgement on the guide's value

questions.explanation: An address presumes one, and unexplained local names show the guide is written for someone who holds
questions.hint: Ask who can follow the guide without explanation.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why an epigraph may be retained even when its context has vanished.
questions.stem: Note 83 on the correspondence novel explains why the translator kept an epigraph whose source the original author never named.

answer.exemplar: The epigraph quotes a line about waiting that the original text attributes to nobody, and its source has been lost. The translator kept it because the line's function does not depend on knowing who wrote it: it frames the letters that follow as a set of delays and unanswered replies, and naming the speaker would only reduce the reader's attention to the correspondence itself.

questions.explanation: An epigraph can work purely by its claim, and a line about waiting frames the correspondence as delays without needing an attribution. The note records that the lost source costs the reader nothing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the missing source matters

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a title's meaning shifts across a translation history.
questions.stem: Translator's note 87 considers how the title of the winter novel changed across two earlier editions and one translation.

options.text: The title narrowed across the editions, so each version was simply a poorer translation of the same phrase.
options.misconception: attributes every change to translation quality

options.text: The title narrowed across the editions, so each version cut away a sense of scale the earlier version carried.
The title widened across the editions, so each version added a sense of scope to the original phrase.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the change

options.text: The title did not change, since publishers reuse an established title to keep the books findable.
options.misconception: assumes commercial continuity overrides editorial change

questions.explanation: Tracing a title across editions shows its sense shrinking, and each cut removes a layer of scale the earlier version carried. Poor translation, reversed direction
questions.hint: Ask what each version drops out of the phrase.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a late image constitutes a payoff or an addition.

stimulus.body: The play translation introduces a single image of a cracked cup in the final exchange, and the image appears nowhere earlier in the text. The translator flagged it because the source edition also carried it, and asked whether a lone image can still function as a payoff.

questions.stem: Translator's note 91 asks whether the cracked cup can function as a payoff in the translated play.

options.text: It cannot, since a payoff by definition requires at least three earlier appearances of the same image.
options.misconception: invents a fixed numeric rule for payoffs

options.text: It cannot, since the image belongs to the source edition and so cannot be the translator's concern.
options.misconception: removes the translator from any responsibility for the text

options.text: It can, since a final image condensing the play's central damage does a payoff's work without recurrence.
It can, since the cracked cup makes the play funnier at the end
options.misconception: reduces a payoff to comic effect

questions.explanation: A payoff condenses the work's central concern into a final image, and that function does not strictly require earlier recurrence. Numeric thresholds, publisher responsibility
questions.hint: Ask whether the image condenses the play's central damage.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how description of a place conveys a character's state.
questions.stem: Translator's note 95 asks how the description of the kitchen in the domestic novel conveys its narrator's state.

options.text: It conveys state through selection, since the kitchen is described as a shambles
options.misconception: reverses which details reveal the state

options.text: It conveys state only through the narrator's declared feelings
options.misconception: excludes description from conveying emotion

options.text: It conveys state through the number of rooms described, since more rooms in a description always mean more.
options.misconception: invents a numeric test for emotional disturbance

options.text: It conveys state through selection, since the kitchen is described as immaculate

questions.explanation: Description conveys feeling through the selection and contrast of details, and an immaculate kitchen beside shaking hands exposes a state never declared. Room counts each miss the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what the contrast between the two details exposes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how an address and a title together position the reader.
questions.stem: Translator's note 99 considers the title and the second-person opening of the letter manual.

options.text: They work together, since the title puts readers in a recipient's place and the second person holds them.
They work together, since the title describes a book and the second person describes a style
options.misconception: treats the pairing as complementary subjects

options.text: They work separately, since a title addresses no one and so cannot interact with a grammatical address.
options.misconception: denies that titles can position one

options.text: They work together, since both devices name a person, so readers can identify the book from its title alone.
options.misconception: reduces the pairing to naming a character

questions.explanation: A title can place the reader in a role and an address can keep the reader in it, so the two cooperate to orient the reader. Complementary subjects, sealed categories, and character naming each miss
questions.hint: Ask what position the reader occupies in each device.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why understatement is a preferred register in a particular kind of text.
questions.stem: Note 103 on the bereavement diary explains why the diarist's plain, undramatic register was kept in translation.

answer.exemplar: The diarist writes about a death in short factual sentences without ever naming grief, and the translator kept that register because the restraint is the grief. An explanatory or sentimental rendering would state what the original makes the reader feel, and a diary's credibility depends on sounding like a person recording their days rather than delivering a conclusion about them.

questions.explanation: Understatement suits a text whose credibility rests on plainness, since the withheld feeling is what readers supply. Sentimentality would double what the original achieves
questions.hint: Ask what readers supply when the writer declines

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how an address shifts when a text is translated for a new readership.
questions.stem: Translator's note 107 considers what happened to the second-person address when the household manual was translated.

options.text: The address stayed the same, since grammatical person is a fixed feature that translators do not alter.
options.misconception: believes translation never touches grammatical choices

options.text: The address shifted since the new readers lack the assumptions behind it, so the translator had to recast.
The address shifted since the new readers find second person unfriendly
options.misconception: grounds the change in reader preference alone

options.text: The address stayed the same, since the manual's readers are told on the first page who the appeals are for.
options.misconception: assumes an explicit statement cancels the address problem

questions.explanation: A translated address has to reach readers who may not hold the assumptions behind the original, so appeals may need recasting. Unalterable person, reader taste
questions.hint: Ask what the new readers may not assume about the appeals.

questions.learningObjective: Compare the effect of an epigraph quoted from another work.

stimulus.body: The memoir translation quotes a line from an older poem above its first chapter, and the poem is credited. The memoir's narrator later argues with the poem's claim in the middle of the book, and the translator wondered whether the credit should stay in the translated edition.

questions.stem: Translator's note 111 asks how the quoted epigraph should be handled in the translation.

options.text: The credit should stay, since every quoted epigraph must name its source or the translation is incomplete.
options.misconception: grounds the practice in a rule of completeness

options.text: The credit should be removed, since a later argument with the quote makes the epigraph an embarrassment.
options.misconception: treats the memoir's disagreement as grounds for suppression

options.text: The credit should stay, since the memoir's argument with the quoted claim is part of what the epigraph sets.
The credit should be removed, since translated editions should use the original language for quotations.
options.misconception: invents a national rule for quoted material

questions.explanation: An epigraph sets up the position the text will later engage, so a memoir that argues with a quoted line shows the epigraph doing its work. Completeness rules, embarrassment
questions.hint: Ask what the memoir later does with the quoted claim.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how a title and an ending together determine a reading.
questions.stem: Translator's note 115 asks how the title and the final scene of the bakery novel should be read together.

options.text: Together they show a life that was only ever about bread, so the sale of the ovens reads as retirement.
options.misconception: reads the title and ending as plain evidence of trade

options.text: Together they show a life that was never about bread, and the title works as a label the ending confirms.
options.misconception: misses the pretence the closing scene exposes

options.text: Together they show nothing, since the translator was told to keep the title's English form.
options.misconception: cites a commercial instruction as a reading

options.text: Together they show a life that was never about bread, so the sale of the ovens ends a pretence.

questions.explanation: Title and ending together reveal the gap between what a life claimed to be about and what it was, and selling the ovens exposes a pretence the title sustained. Plain trade, label and confirmation
questions.hint: Ask what the sale of the ovens reveals about the title.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the constraint a motif's payoff places on a translator.
questions.stem: Translator's note 118 observes that the final return of the ferry rope in the island novel depends on a specific verb.

options.text: The payoff depends on a verb of letting go, since the rope is finally uncoiled rather than pulled.
The payoff depends on a verb of pulling, since the rope is finally pulled clear of the water as it was before.
options.misconception: ignores the reversal in the action described

options.text: The payoff depends on the verb untied, since the knot is finally untied rather than retied as it was before.
options.misconception: confuses the knot's action with the verb that matters

options.text: The payoff does not depend on any verb, since a returning image carries meaning whatever word is chosen.
options.misconception: assumes images are immune to lexical choice

questions.explanation: A payoff often turns on a word that reverses the motif's earlier action, and letting go against repeated pulling is that reversal. The other verbs either preserve the old action or shift the question
questions.hint: Ask how the final action differs from the earlier ones.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a description of weather carries the reader's sympathy.
questions.stem: Note 121 on the coastal novel records how the translator handled the long description of the storm in the middle chapters.

answer.exemplar: The description of the storm runs to several paragraphs and never names what any character feels, so the translator preserved its length and its refusal of comment. Because the weather is given the weight that feeling would normally take, the reader supplies the fear and the pity for the boats, and any rendering that named those feelings would take that work away from the reader rather than do it for them.

questions.explanation: Description that occupies the place of stated feeling transfers the emotional work to the reader. Preserving the storm's length and its refusal to comment keeps that transfer intact.
questions.hint: Ask who supplies the feeling the description leaves out.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how two devices together produce an effect neither could make alone.
questions.stem: Translator's note 125 considers the pairing of an understatement and an epigraph in the medicine novel.

options.text: Together they build a case, since the epigraph states the claim and the flat narration repeats it in plainer.
options.misconception: reduces the pairing to restatement of one idea

options.text: Together they build a case, since the epigraph states the claim and the flat narration then quietly refuses
They work separately, since an epigraph makes a claim while understatement is only a matter of word choice.
options.misconception: confines understatement to a lexical matter

options.text: They work separately, since the translator was asked to keep the epigraph and the body stylistically uniform.
options.misconception: invents a uniformity instruction to separate them

questions.explanation: When an epigraph asserts a claim and the narration declines to endorse it, the two devices together build an argument
questions.hint: Ask whether the narration agrees with the epigraph's claim.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise understatement carried by the arrangement of events rather than by wording.

stimulus.body: In the small-town novel, a boy's father is described leaving on a Tuesday morning in one paragraph and never returning in the text. The translator's note records that the original makes no statement about the departure and that the community goes on with its business in the very next chapter.

questions.stem: Translator's note 129 asks where the understatement in this novel actually sits.

options.text: It sits in the arrangement, since the father returns at the end and the town has pretended all along
options.misconception: invents a return that the note does not mention

options.text: It sits in the wording, since the original uses a specific soft phrase for leaving
options.misconception: confines understatement to one lexical choice

options.text: It sits in the arrangement, since a departure of that kind is stated once in small terms and the town's life.
It sits nowhere, since the community continuing its business shows the departure carried no emotional weight.
options.misconception: reads a designed effect as an absence of weight

questions.explanation: Understatement can be structural, and a departure stated once and absorbed by the town's routine diminishes the event. An invented return and a lexical focus each miss that work.
questions.hint: Ask what the text chooses not to say about the departure.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a text's address changes what its narrator can claim.
questions.stem: Translator's note 133 asks whether the manual's address to a beginner limits what its narrator may assert.

options.text: It limits the assertions, since a voice that assumes a beginner cannot admit uncertainty in case readers lose.
options.misconception: makes the address a constraint on candour alone

options.text: It does not limit the assertions, since a narrator may speak
options.misconception: denies that address can constrain a narrator

options.text: It does not limit the assertions, since the address only positions readers and never touches the narrator's.
options.misconception: insists that address and assertion are wholly separate

options.text: It limits the assertions, since a voice assuming a beginner cannot assert specialist facts unexplained.

questions.explanation: Addressing beginners obliges a narrator to explain specialist material, so the presumed reader constrains what may be asserted. Candour alone and free assertion each misdescribe the constraint.
questions.hint: Ask what the presumed reader forces the narrator to explain.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how an epigraph can narrow the interpretations a reader allows.
questions.stem: Translator's note 137 explains why the epigraph of the drowned village novel closes off one common reading.

options.text: It closes the reading off since the epigraph insists the village was never a place of happiness, ruling out.
It closes the reading off since the epigraph names the year of the flood, so the chronology is fixed.
options.misconception: explains the narrowing as chronological restriction

options.text: It closes the reading off since the epigraph is a quotation from a critic
options.misconception: grounds the narrowing in attribution alone

options.text: It does not close anything off, since an epigraph in a translated novel is only a decorative flourish.
options.misconception: denies any interpretive force to epigraphs

questions.explanation: An epigraph can forbid a reading by asserting the opposite of it, and a denial of happiness rules out nostalgia as the book's mode. Dating, attribution, and decorative status each miss how it narrows.
questions.hint: Ask what the epigraph asserts that one cannot then claim.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a title's question is answered by an ending.
questions.stem: Note 141 on the railway novel explains how the closing scene answers the question posed by the title.

answer.exemplar: The title asks who waits at the end of the line, and the novel closes on a stationmaster who has waited every working day of his life for a train that the timetable says no longer runs. The scene answers the title by refusing the question's premise: someone does wait, and the waiting has been the whole of his occupation, which is why the ending reads as an indictment rather than an answer.

questions.explanation: A title's question is answered by what the ending shows, and a man still waiting for a discontinued service answers who waits worst. The ending refuses the title's hope, which makes it an indictment.
questions.hint: Ask who is still waiting when the novel ends.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a translator may keep a motif whose payoff the source withholds.
questions.stem: Translator's note 145 considers the recurrent image of the shut window in the source text of the lodging novel.

options.text: The translator may keep it, since an unresolved motif is only unfinished work and translators should supply.
options.misconception: obliges translators to complete the source text

options.text: The translator may keep it, since an unresolved motif still shapes the reading even when the source declines
The translator must drop it, since a motif without a payoff misleads the reader about what the work is doing.
options.misconception: treats an open motif as a false promise

options.text: The translator must drop it, since motifs are culturally specific and cannot survive a change of language.
options.misconception: assumes motifs cannot be carried across languages

questions.explanation: An unresolved motif still organises readers' sense of the text even when the source refuses to close it, so it may be kept. Completion duties, false promises
questions.hint: Ask whether the image still shapes the reading on its own.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of a room that is described only after it has been left.

stimulus.body: The retirement novel describes a man's kitchen only in the chapter after he has died in it, and the translator's rendering keeps the description in the present tense for a few sentences before shifting to the past. The editorial team asked what the tense shift is doing there.

questions.stem: Translator's note 149 asks what the shift from present to past tense achieves in the kitchen description.

options.text: It lets the reader understand the kitchen's layout better
options.misconception: reads a tense shift as improved clarity

options.text: It warns the reader that the information is secondhand, so the present tense marks the narrator's uncertainty.
options.misconception: treats tense as a marker of evidential doubt

options.text: It lets the reader stand briefly inside the room as it was, so the dead man's kitchen arrives as a place.
It has no effect, since tense in a description of a room is a matter of grammar rather than of effect.
options.misconception: denies that grammar can carry feeling

questions.explanation: A brief present tense makes the room feel still inhabited and the description an arrival into a preserved space, so the shift works emotionally. Clarity, evidential doubt
questions.hint: Ask where readers are standing during those few sentences.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how a translator's decisions can combine to change a work's tone.
questions.stem: Translator's note 153 asks what the combination of a shortened epigraph and a warmer rendering did to the memoir.

options.text: It made the memoir feel more encouraging, since the epigraph now agrees with the warmer prose and supports.
options.misconception: misses the loss of productive disagreement

options.text: It left the memoir's tone unchanged, since epigraphs and prose affect separate parts of a book.
options.misconception: denies that devices interact across a text

options.text: It left the memoir's tone unchanged, since tone is fixed by the author and no translation choice can alter it.
options.misconception: treats tone as immune to translation

options.text: It made the memoir feel more encouraging, since the epigraph stopped pressing the doubt the prose softened.

questions.explanation: When an epigraph's doubt is removed and the prose is warmed, the disagreement that made the memoir interesting disappears and the result reads as encouragement. Direct agreement, separate domains
questions.hint: Ask what argument the shortened epigraph no longer makes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how understatement differs from vagueness in a translated passage.
questions.stem: Translator's note 157 explains why the phrase some damage to the workshop was kept as a rendering of the original.

options.text: It is understatement since the reader knows how much damage occurred
It is understatement since readers have no idea how much damage occurred
options.misconception: confuses understatement with deliberate vagueness

options.text: It is vagueness since the phrase could describe any amount of damage, so it commits the translator to nothing.
options.misconception: reads measured restraint as an absence of commitment

options.text: It is neither, since a phrase describing damage in a workshop novel carries no figurative charge.
options.misconception: denies figurative weight to literal description

questions.explanation: Understatement is smallness measured against a known scale, and readers' knowledge of the actual damage makes the modest phrase deliberate. Vagueness, no commitment
questions.hint: Ask what the reader knows about the scale.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a text addresses a reader it never names.
questions.stem: Note 161 on the readers' manual explains how the text addresses an implied reader through its examples.

answer.exemplar: The manual never names its reader, but every example uses a person of a particular kind: one who has a say in a household budget and is answerable to others for it. That repeated choice of example addresses an implied reader without ever using the second person, so the manual's instructions reach someone who is neither a child nor a stranger but a person carrying household responsibility.

questions.explanation: A text can address an implied reader through the situations it chooses to illustrate. Consistent examples carry the address without any pronoun
questions.hint: Ask who the manual keeps imagining when it gives examples.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether an epigraph sets a tone that the rest of the text sustains.
questions.stem: Translator's note 165 asks whether the wry epigraph of the almanac novel is sustained by the chapters that follow.

options.text: It is sustained, since the epigraph was written by the author, so the chapters must match it by definition.
options.misconception: grounds continuity in authorship rather than in the prose

options.text: It is sustained, since the chapters keep the same wry distance
It is not sustained, since the chapters grow sombre and the early epigraph promises a lightness the book.
options.misconception: misses a change of register the translator notes elsewhere

options.text: It is not sustained, since translated editions replace an author's epigraph with one of the publisher's.
options.misconception: makes publisher replacement the default practice

questions.explanation: An epigraph's tone sets a promise the text must keep, and a wry distance maintained across the chapters shows
questions.hint: Ask what the chapters' manner does with the epigraph's.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a title's ambiguity is resolved or left open by an ending.

stimulus.body: The title of the newspaper novel is The Second Edition, and it can mean the reprinted issue or the revised life of the woman who wrote the front page. The last chapter describes her reprinting the paper with a correction that removes the editor she wrote against. The translator recorded both readings as possible.

questions.stem: Translator's note 169 asks how the ending bears on the two possible readings of the title.

options.text: It settles the title on the first reading, since a reprinted issue is the only thing the last chapter.
options.misconception: ignores the second possible sense of the title

options.text: It settles the title on the second reading, since a revised life is the only thing the last chapter describes.
options.misconception: ignores the first possible sense of the title

options.text: It bears on both, since a corrected reissue serves as a reprinted issue and a revised account of one woman's.
It settles nothing, since a title with two possible senses can never be clarified by any ending.
options.misconception: assumes ambiguity is permanently unresolvable

questions.explanation: An ending can bear on every sense a title carries, and a corrected reprint serves simultaneously as an issue and as a revised life. Exclusive readings and permanent ambiguity each fail
questions.hint: Ask what the reissued paper is at the same time.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how a motif's payoff and a work's central question converge.
questions.stem: Translator's note 173 asks how the return of the unposted letter answers the novel's central question.

options.text: It answers it definitively, since a letter that stays unposted ends the enquiry the novel began.
options.misconception: reads an unresolved image as a definitive answer

options.text: It answers it by shifting the question to a different character
options.misconception: mistakes a change of subject for an answer

options.text: It answers nothing, since the central question of a novel is answered by its plot and never by a recurring.
options.misconception: confines a work's answers to plot mechanics

options.text: It answers it by keeping the question open in a new form, since the unposted letter repeats the silence.

questions.explanation: A payoff can re-present a question rather than close it, and an unposted letter repeats the silence the novel has been examining in a new form. Definitive closure, redirected attention
questions.hint: Ask what the unposted letter repeats rather than settles.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a setting can carry an argument rather than a mood.
questions.stem: Translator's note 177 considers whether the border village described in the novel's first and last pages carries an argument.

options.text: It carries an argument, since a village astride a line
It carries only a mood, since a setting can colour a scene but never take a position of its own.
options.misconception: denies that a setting can make a claim

options.text: It carries an argument, since a village divided by a border proves
options.misconception: reads a narrator's situation as the translator's opinion

options.text: It carries only a mood, since the translator was asked
options.misconception: cites an accuracy instruction to avoid interpretation

questions.explanation: A setting can make a claim, and a narrator who crosses a border daily can argue about belonging without ever stating it. Mood only, translator opinion
questions.hint: Ask what the narrator's crossing makes true about belonging.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a translator's note can itself perform a literary function.
questions.stem: Note 181 on the anthology explains why the translator wrote a note at all rather than leaving the choices unremarked.

answer.exemplar: The translator wrote the note because the alternative was worse: a reader who met a rendered word without explanation would assume it was the only word available, and would carry that false certainty into reading the rest of the story. The note therefore does the same work the epigraph does in the text, telling the reader how to approach what follows, and refusing to explain would have been the greater distortion.

questions.explanation: A translator's note is a framing device as much as a record, and it teaches the reader how to approach the text rather than documenting choices. Silence would have produced a worse misreading.
questions.hint: Ask what one would wrongly assume without the note.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse the effect of understatement in a document that reports numbers.
questions.stem: Translator's note 184 asks why the report in the famine novel gives a total of nine hundred without further comment.

options.text: The flatness works since a bare figure is standard practice in official reports and readers expect no comment.
options.misconception: explains the effect by convention rather than by force

options.text: The flatness works since the plain figure carries more weight than any accompanying description would.
The flatness works since the figure is so small that no reader could be moved by such a small number.
options.misconception: suggests the number is trivial rather than damning

options.text: The flatness fails, since a report that means
options.misconception: requires an explicit moral statement to be effective

questions.explanation: A bare figure in a document about deaths exerts more force than description would, since the refusal to editorialise is itself the accusation. Convention, triviality
questions.hint: Ask what the absence of comment is itself saying.

questions.learningObjective: Identify how an address can be built from vocabulary rather than pronouns.

stimulus.body: The garden manual uses no second person at all. It speaks of the gardener and the soil and the pruning in the third person throughout, and the translator's note observes that the effect is still one of instruction. The question put to the translator was how a text can address someone without using you.

questions.stem: Translator's note 188 asks how the garden manual addresses its reader without a pronoun.

options.text: It addresses the reader through its subject matter, since a text about gardens is by definition addressed
options.misconception: grounds the address in subject matter alone

options.text: It does not address the reader, since addressing requires a pronoun and the manual contains no second person.
options.misconception: makes pronouns a necessary condition of address

options.text: It addresses the reader through the choices the manual imagines the reader making
It does not address readers, since the third person suggests the manual describes a gardener, not a guide.
options.misconception: reads third person as description only

questions.explanation: A text addresses readers by the decisions it imagines for them, and a manual whose subject is always the person choosing is addressed to the chooser. Subject matter, pronoun necessity
questions.hint: Ask who the manual keeps making decisions for.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how epigraphs work across a multi-part work.
questions.stem: Translator's note 192 asks what the three epigraphs of the three volumes do for the trilogy's structure.

options.text: They build an argument, since all three epigraphs state the same claim and reinforce the thesis.
options.misconception: misses the progression from claim to answer to openness

options.text: They organise nothing, since epigraphs in a multi-part work are chosen by each volume's editor independently.
options.misconception: assumes each part's framing is decided in isolation

options.text: They organise nothing, since a trilogy repeating its epigraphs signals a lack of new material in the later.
options.misconception: reads a planned sequence as mere repetition

options.text: They build an argument, since each epigraph answers the one before and the third leaves the sequence open.

questions.explanation: A sequence of epigraphs can develop its own argument, answering and reopening across the parts, and that is what these three do. Repetition, independent choosing
questions.hint: Ask what the third epigraph does with the first two.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a title's repetition in a sequence of volumes structures a work.
questions.stem: Translator's note 196 notes that the second volume of the sequence is titled The Second Book of Hours with the same title as its predecessor.

options.text: The shared title links the volumes and marks the second as a continuation of the same office
The shared title is a publishing shortcut, since reprinting a title sells better than inventing a new one.
options.misconception: explains the repetition by commercial motive

options.text: The shared title suggests the second volume repeats the first, so readers should expect identical material.
options.misconception: infers identical content from a repeated title

options.text: The shared title separates the volumes, since a second book of the same name must be read against the first.
options.misconception: turns a linking title into a contrastive device

questions.explanation: A repeated title can mark continuity across volumes, and naming a second book of the same office tells the reader this is a continuation. Selling, identical content
questions.hint: Ask what the number in the title tells the reader.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a motif can carry across separate volumes of a work.
questions.stem: Note 200 on the two-volume account asks how the image of the sealed tin continues from the first volume into the second.

answer.exemplar: The sealed tin appears once in the first volume, in the hands of a woman who closes it and puts it on a high shelf, and the translator kept the image unglossed so that it would carry no explanation across the gap between the volumes. In the second volume the tin is found and opened, and because the earlier appearance was never explained, its opening settles an old debt in a way that the reader supplies entirely.

questions.explanation: A motif that crosses a gap between volumes needs no explanation if its earlier appearance was left plain, since readers supply the connection. Glossing it would fix a meaning the payoff must fight.
questions.hint: Ask why the first appearance was left without explanation.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a description of a place changes when the person describing it changes.
questions.stem: Translator's note 204 compares the description of the same house in the early and late chapters of the estate novel.

options.text: The later description is colder since the house itself has been altered by the renovations in the middle.
options.misconception: attributes the change to the building rather than the owner

options.text: The later description is colder since the owner has changed, so the same rooms register a colder regard.
The later description is warmer since time has softened the owner, so the same rooms invite more notice.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the change in regard

options.text: The descriptions are identical in effect, since a house is a house and readers' judgement of it cannot change.
options.misconception: denies that a repeated place can be revalued

questions.explanation: A repeated place is revalued by the person who describes it, and a colder owner makes the same rooms register colder. Renovations, warmth, and fixed judgement each miss
questions.hint: Ask who is looking at the rooms the second time.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate how an address and a title can work against each other.

stimulus.body: The pamphlet translation is titled A Letter to My Successor and is written throughout in the second person, addressing the person who will take over the work. In the final page the writer explains that no successor exists and that the pamphlet was never posted. The translator noted that the address and the ending pull against each other.

questions.stem: Translator's note 208 explains how the pamphlet's address and its ending pull against each other.

options.text: The address and the ending agree, since both are about the pamphlet being addressed
options.misconception: misses the tension the translator recorded

options.text: The address is the defect, since a pamphlet should never be written to a successor when no successor exists.
options.misconception: treats the fictional address as an error to be fixed

options.text: The address builds one and the ending withdraws it, so the second person becomes a fiction the pamphlet.
There is no tension, since the second person in a pamphlet always refers to the writer's own later self.
options.misconception: assigns a fixed referent to the second person

questions.explanation: An address creates a presumed reader and an ending that denies the address's premise withdraws that reader, which is the tension here. Agreement, defect, and a fixed referent each miss the exposure.
questions.hint: Ask what the second person assumes and the ending removes.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how understatement works across a translator's whole rendering.
questions.stem: Translator's note 212 asks what the consistently restrained register of the translation does for the memoir.

options.text: It produces a cumulative quiet, since each small measured sentence tells the reader less than the memoir.
options.misconception: confuses cumulative effect with uniform omission

options.text: It produces nothing, since understatement only works in single lines and cannot accumulate across a whole.
options.misconception: confines understatement to short passages

options.text: It produces a memoir that sounds guarded
options.misconception: turns a register into an accusation of the translator

options.text: It produces a cumulative quiet, since each small measured sentence leaves a residue readers accumulate across.

questions.explanation: Understatement accumulates, and a register of measured sentences leaves a residue that builds across the book. Uniform omission, short-passage limits
questions.hint: Ask what one carries forward after each small sentence.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an address that invites from one that instructs.
questions.stem: Translator's note 216 describes the difference between the invitations of the recipe book and the instructions of the safety card.

options.text: The invitation leaves readers free to refuse, whereas the instruction presumes a compliance agreed to.
The invitation demands obedience, whereas the instruction leaves the reader free to accept or refuse it.
options.misconception: reverses which register carries compulsion

options.text: Both forms address the same reader, so the difference between them is only one of politeness.
options.misconception: reduces the difference to manner of speaking

options.text: Both forms address no one, since instructions and invitations are written for the writer's own reference.
options.misconception: denies address in instructional texts

questions.explanation: An invitation presumes readers may decline while an instruction presumes agreement given, and the two forms expect different responses. Politeness, reversal
questions.hint: Ask what each form assumes readers have agreed to.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a translator records an epigraph's presence in the note.
questions.stem: Note 220 on the pamphlet collection explains why the translator's note lists the epigraphs separately from the other front matter.

answer.exemplar: The translator listed the epigraphs apart because they are not decorative. An epigraph sets a position the text then tests, so a reader who treats it as a motto, or skips it as an ornament, will misread what follows. By isolating the epigraphs in the note the translator gives the reader the habit of reading them as arguments, which is the only way the front matter of the collection can be made to do its work.

questions.explanation: Front matter like an epigraph shapes the reading of everything after it, and calling attention to it trains the reader to treat it as argument rather than ornament. Isolating it in the note protects
questions.hint: Ask what one loses by treating an epigraph as a motto.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a translation's title affects the reading of the ending.
questions.stem: Translator's note 224 considers what the English title makes of the novel's final chapter.

options.text: It makes the ending a departure, since the English title names a place the last chapter finally leaves behind.
options.misconception: reverses the relation between the title and the arrival

options.text: It makes the ending an arrival, since the English title names a place the last chapter finally reaches.
It makes the ending an arrival, since the last chapter repeats the title word in its last sentence.
options.misconception: credits a repeated word for the reading effect

options.text: It makes no difference, since a title is a label and the ending supplies the meaning on its own.
options.misconception: treats the title as inert in the reading

questions.explanation: A title that names a destination makes the last chapter an arrival, and the reader arrives with the title in hand. Departure, a repeated word and inert labels each miss how the title frames the close.
questions.hint: Ask what the English title makes the reader expect.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the constraint that a motif's payoff places on earlier description.

stimulus.body: The novel translation describes a garden gate in the middle chapters with a great deal of attention to the latch, its weight and the difficulty of operating it. The final chapter reveals that the gate was never locked and that the characters were simply afraid to open it. The translator marked the descriptive passages for checking in the new edition.

questions.stem: Translator's note 228 asks why the translator marked the earlier garden-gate passages for checking.

options.text: Because the description contains an error, since a gate that was never locked should not have been described.
options.misconception: reads the emphasis as a factual mistake about weight

options.text: Because the final revelation shows the description was unnecessary
options.misconception: confuses a change in reading with a reason to delete

options.text: Because the final revelation changes how the detailed description reads
Because the translator wanted to add a note explaining the latch's significance once the ending was known.
options.misconception: jumps to annotation rather than weighing the emphasis

questions.explanation: A payoff can change the significance of earlier description, so the translator had to weigh whether the emphasis on the latch still served the reading. Errors, deletions
questions.hint: Ask what the revelation does to the earlier emphasis.

questions.learningObjective: Judge how a translator's treatment of setting shapes a reader's sympathy.
questions.stem: Translator's note 232 asks how the rendering of the crowded waiting room in the clinic novel shapes sympathy.

options.text: It shapes sympathy toward the waiting people, since the description gives their illnesses detail
options.misconception: swaps which of the two details carries the feeling

options.text: It shapes sympathy away from the waiting people, since a crowded description makes them a crowd and crowds.
options.misconception: assumes collective description prevents individual sympathy

options.text: It shapes no sympathy, since a translator's job is to reproduce the room and not to arrange readers' feelings.
options.misconception: cites the translator's remit to rule out effect

options.text: It shapes sympathy toward the waiting people, since the description gives their discomfort detail

questions.explanation: Sympathy follows the details a description chooses to develop, and giving discomfort detail
questions.hint: Ask which of the two details receives readers' attention.
